beats.vo: On the fifth of January ten sixty-six, King Edward of England died with no clear heir. The richest and most powerful noble in the kingdom, Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, was elected king and crowned.

beats.vo: He was challenged at once by two powerful neighbours. Across the Channel, William, Duke of Normandy. Across the North Sea, Harald Hardrada, King of Norway.

beats.vo: William claimed that Edward had promised him the throne, and that Harold had sworn to support that promise. The Bayeux Tapestry, probably commissioned by Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, soon after the battle, shows Harold swearing an oath to William.

beats.vo: Hardrada's claim rested on an agreement between his predecessor, Magnus the Good, and an earlier king of England, Harthacnut. Whichever of them died without an heir, the other would inherit both kingdoms. Both William and Hardrada began to gather ships.

beats.vo: Harold spent the summer on the south coast with an army and a fleet, waiting for William. But most of his men were militia who had harvests to bring in. On the eighth of September he sent the militia and the fleet home.

beats.vo: That same month, Hardrada invaded the north with more than three hundred ships, carrying perhaps fifteen thousand men, joined by Harold's own exiled brother, Tostig. On the twentieth of September, at Fulford, just south of York, they defeated the northern earls and took the city.

beats.vo: Harold rushed north, gathering men as he went, and caught the Norwegians by surprise at Stamford Bridge on the twenty-fifth of September. Hardrada and Tostig were both killed. Of the three hundred ships, only twenty-four were needed to carry the survivors home.

beats.vo: The battle has traditionally been called the end of the Viking Age. But the victory came at great cost. Harold's army was battered and weakened, and far from the south. Three days later, William landed.

beats.vo: William had spent almost nine months building a fleet from nothing. He was ready to cross from Saint-Valery-sur-Somme by about the twelfth of August, but the crossing was delayed. On the twenty-eighth of September, with the English fleet gone, the Normans landed at Pevensey.

beats.vo: They built a wooden castle at Hastings and raided the country around it. The exact size of William's army is unknown. Writers at the time gave figures as high as a hundred and fifty thousand. Modern historians estimate between seven and twelve thousand.

beats.vo: About half of William's force was infantry, a quarter cavalry, and a quarter archers or crossbowmen. The English fought on foot: the fyrd, a levy of local landholders, and the housecarls, the king's own armoured men. They had few archers. Their numbers are unknown too, with estimates from five to thirteen thousand.

beats.vo: Harold marched south, stopped in London for about a week, and on the night of the thirteenth of October camped on Caldbec Hill. The battle began the next morning at nine o'clock, between two hills, in country that was heavily wooded, with a marsh nearby.

beats.vo: The English formed a shield wall along the top of a steep slope, shields close together or overlapping, their flanks protected by woods and marshy ground. Below them William drew up three divisions: Bretons on the left, Normans in the centre under William himself, French and Flemings on the right.

beats.vo: The Norman archers opened, shooting uphill into the shield wall, to little effect. The infantry went in next and met a storm of spears, axes and stones. The cavalry followed and could not break through either.

beats.vo: Then a general retreat began, blamed on the Bretons on William's left. A rumour ran through the army that William had been killed. He rode through his men with his face showing, shouting that he was alive, and led a counter-attack on the English who had chased them downhill.

beats.vo: In the afternoon, the Normans appear to have turned that into a tactic: the feigned flight, a pretend retreat to draw men out of the line. Some historians have argued the story was invented afterwards, but most agree it happened. It probably thinned the housecarls, and the fyrd filled the gaps. The wall held.

beats.vo: Late in the day, Harold was killed. How, nobody can say for certain. The Bayeux Tapestry shows a man pulling an arrow from his eye beside a man cut down by a sword, under the words: Here King Harold has been killed. It does not say which one is Harold.

data.title: How did Harold die?
data.sub: An arrow to the eye: first written in the 1080s, Amatus of Montecassino. · Killed by William himself: the Carmen. Unlikely. · 'No one knew who killed him': the Chronicle of Battle Abbey.

beats.vo: With the king dead, the English began to collapse. Many fled. The men of the royal household gathered around Harold's body and fought to the end. A last stand at a place remembered as the Malfosse, the evil ditch, wounded Count Eustace of Boulogne before it too was overrun.

beats.vo: England did not surrender at once. The surviving leaders proclaimed the young Edgar Atheling king. William marched on London, was held at London Bridge, and went the long way round: west to cross the Thames at Wallingford, then towards the city from the north-west. At Berkhamsted the English leaders submitted.

beats.vo: Resistance went on for years: rebellions in Exeter, in the south and west, and in Northumbria, and a Danish fleet. William put them down ruthlessly, ending in the Harrying of the North in the winter of ten sixty-nine. He founded an abbey on the battlefield. Its high altar, later writers said, stood where Harold fell.
